title: European Business survey: Bridging the gap between geopolitics and corporate strategy
gist: A pilot survey of 228 companies operating in Europe (Bertelsmann Stiftung, Clingendael, FIIA, MERICS; fielded Nov 2025-Jan 2026) finds firms slow to integrate economic security into strategy, badly unprepared for a Taiwan contingency, most hurt by US tariffs, and preferring supportive EU policy (Single Market, innovation, industrial policy) over assertive measures against China or the US, revealing a gap with EU policymakers.

themes.theme: Low corporate integration of geopolitical risk

insights.claim: Only about one third of European-operating companies surveyed discuss economic security at management level at least monthly, suggesting geopolitical risk is not yet embedded in corporate strategy.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect under-hedged supply chains and larger earnings shocks from geopolitical events; favour firms that disclose concrete resilience planning.
insights.quote: Only one third of the respondents discuss this issue at management level at least monthly
insights.locator: Awareness of economic security leaves room

insights.claim: The most common geopolitical risk mitigation measures among European-operating firms are diversifying markets (58%), localising production (34%) and stockpiling critical inputs (31%).
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Market diversification dominates over costlier reshoring; demand tailwinds for localisation/automation and inventory build are real but secondary.
insights.locator: The most common measures for mitigating

insights.claim: Despite geopolitical upheaval, surveyed companies have been slow to integrate economic security into their corporate strategies, according to the joint Bertelsmann/Clingendael/FIIA/MERICS survey.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Corporate complacency means shocks are likely to be priced late; watch for sudden guidance cuts when escalations hit.
insights.quote: respondent companies have been slow to integrate this issue into their corporate strategies

themes.theme: US-China rivalry exposure and staying power

insights.claim: 31% of surveyed European-operating firms reported at least one negative impact from the US-China rivalry, yet more than half do not plan to reduce involvement in either the US or Chinese market.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: European corporates are not decoupling from either superpower; revenue exposure to both markets will persist, keeping them vulnerable to bilateral escalation.
insights.locator: At least one negative impact from the US-China rivalry

insights.claim: US tariffs and import quotas are seen by European-operating firms as the most burdensome economic security measure, with 66% reporting a negative impact, significantly higher than for Chinese or EU measures.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: For European exporters, Washington's trade policy is currently the bigger margin risk than Beijing's; weight US tariff headlines more heavily for EU industrials.
insights.quote: US tariffs/import quotas are seen as the most burdensome economic security measure, with 66% having reported a negative impact

insights.claim: Only 10% of surveyed European-operating companies have taken concrete preparations for a Taiwan contingency, even though around 81% experienced or expect tangible effects from Russia's war against Ukraine.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A Taiwan crisis would hit a largely unprepared European corporate base; tail-risk hedges on EU equities with Asian supply dependence are underpriced by management.
insights.quote: Respondents are largely unprepared for a Taiwan contingency: Only 10% reported having taken concrete preparations
insights.locator: Respondents are largely unprepared for a Taiwan

insights.claim: The survey authors urge companies to improve preparedness for geopolitical contingencies, including Taiwan-related disruptions and spillover effects from regional conflicts.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Watch for EU guidance or stress-test regimes pushing firms toward Taiwan scenario planning, which could drive inventory and sourcing shifts.

themes.theme: Business vs policymaker gap on EU response

insights.claim: Companies' top priorities for EU action are strengthening the Single Market (61%), investment in technological innovation (59%) and a more coherent industrial policy (53%), while more assertive measures against China (18%) or the United States (16%) get limited support.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Business lobbying will resist aggressive EU trade defence; Single Market and innovation-funding initiatives have the broadest corporate backing.
insights.locator: Respondents' top priorities for EU action

insights.claim: Corporate preference for supportive rather than assertive economic security measures reveals a gap between companies and EU policymakers on what is needed to secure Europe's economic security.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect friction and possible dilution when the EU rolls out protective tools; policy outcomes may be less hawkish than Brussels rhetoric.
insights.quote: corporate preference for supportive rather than assertive measures reveals a gap between companies and EU policymakers

insights.claim: The authors recommend the EU prepare targeted protective measures against unfair competition and power-play tactics from both the United States and China, while acknowledging this will likely draw disapproval from parts of the business community.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Think-tank consensus is pushing Brussels toward trade-defence tools aimed at both Washington and Beijing; monitor for anti-coercion or countermeasure moves.

insights.claim: Proposed EU policy priorities include clearer economic security guidance, advisory support for SMEs, and regular geopolitical stress tests for strategically important firms.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Geopolitical stress tests for strategic firms could become a new compliance layer, analogous to bank stress tests, affecting disclosure and capex.

insights.claim: The authors call for trusted channels for confidential data exchange between governments and businesses to enable evidence-based economic security policy.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Signals more government visibility into corporate supply-chain data, potentially preceding targeted interventions in dependent sectors.
insights.locator: Establishing trusted channels for the confidential

insights.claim: Recommended corporate approach: identify vulnerabilities in key inputs, then diversify where necessary, stockpile where critical and factor in supply chain disruptions so resilience becomes a core strength.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Useful checklist for evaluating management quality on geopolitical risk in European holdings.
insights.locator: Integrating economic security into strategic planning

insights.claim: The pilot survey covered 228 companies operating in Europe (around 130-150 answering most questions), was fielded November 2025 to January 2026 with BusinessEurope distributing it, predates recent transatlantic escalations and the Iran conflict, and is not statistically representative.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Treat findings as directional; corporate sentiment on US measures and conflict risk has likely worsened since fieldwork.
insights.locator: The survey was conducted between November 2025
